newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's Cetes rates fall on stable peso, prices.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's Cetes rates fall on stable peso, prices.

text.p: Investors in Mexico's primary Cetes, sensing lower inflation and a stable peso, drove down yields across the curve at the primary treasury bill auction on Tuesday, market analysts said.
The rate on bellwether one-month paper fell a sharp 201 basis points to 23.46 percent, below market expectations.
Demand rose sharply, to 15.12 billion pesos, with a bid-to-cover ratio of 4.58. Foreign investors were seen behind the strong demand.
Banco de Mexico said on Monday that inflation for August was 1.33 percent, slightly below expectations.
Many investors are also starting to sense inflation could be stable for the rest of the year and into early 1997.
The peso has also remained in a tight range, with the spot 48-hour peso contract ending the day on Tuesday at 7.55/7.555 per dollar.
Bancomer economist Javier Maldonado said market watchers expected it to remain below 8.0 per dollar at the end of the year.
"These two things, the stable peso and lower inflation expectations, have contributed to the lower interest rates," said Maldonado.
Demand was particularly heavy at 4.35 billion pesos for the 90-day paper, which yielded 164 basis points less than last week, falling to 27.73 percent this week.
Demand on the 182-day paper was 4.83 billion pesos, and the yield fell 183 basis points to 29.91 percent.
One-year paper yielded 30.93 percent this week, compared to 32.43 percent last week on demand of 3.16 billion pesos this week.
Banco de Mexico auctioned all 3.3 billion pesos worth of Cetes offered.
"It is probable that the increase in demand had a lot to do with the participation of foreigners, especially in the 90-day paper," said Ricardo Vazquez, an analyst with Banco Union.
However, analysts said they doubt rates can fall much further.
"They can't fall that much more unless there is a better economic and political picture," said Maldonado, adding, however, that there is some room for more declines on the longer-term paper.
